title: IAG, Suncorp in frame for $20bn Tokio Marine play
full_text:
Insurance Australia Group and Suncorp are understood to be in the crosshairs of Japanese insurer Tokio Marine for a buyout, in what would be a $20bn-plus transaction should one proceed.
DataRoom understands that IAG has Goldman Sachs in its corner for any negotiations.
IAG said that it had not received any inbound approaches from the Japanese group and declined to comment further.
However, the understanding is that the Japanese suitor is motivated to embark on a transaction to put excess capital to work, and analysts say it told the market about a month ago it wanted to break into the Australian or Canadian market with a big buy.
IAG becomes a candidate as it has largely resolved its major legal exposure to the collapse of Greensill Capital by agreeing to a confidential settlement of the $4bn Greensill Bank lawsuit.
IAG’s share price is up 7 per cent year to date but has been steady for the past year, while Suncorp is up 8 per cent this year and down 6 per cent over the past year.
Both groups have market values of about $20bn.
While one source has pointed to IAG as Tokio Marine’s target, another believes Suncorp is in its sights, while one market expert said it was also sizing up Hollard.
Some say the group, which is listed in Japan with a value of about $140bn, is testing the possibility of buying either company.
Founded in 1879, Tokio Marine Group is a global insurer operating in more than 50 countries and regions with over 50,000 employees worldwide.
Suncorp has been close to Barrenjoey, UBS and JPMorgan.
Insurers are likely on heightened alert when it comes to interest from suitors amid buoyant times for the industry.
Companies globally are reaping a windfall from inflation-fuelled price increases to consumers, justified partly by the threat of catastrophic events brought on by climate change. As a result, they have recorded near-record profits and prospered on the back of higher interest rates, as their cash holdings generate more earnings.
A deal for Suncorp would come after the divestment of its banking arm to ANZ for $4.9bn, announced in 2022.
Suncorp describes itself as a leading insurer offering home, contents and car insurance, whereas IAG says it is the largest general insurer in Australia and New Zealand, providing cover under a range of leading brands.
DataRoom reported in February speculation that IAG could be positioning to sell its intermediated insurance business, which could be worth between $4bn and $5bn, although IAG denied this at the time.
Suncorp, run by Steve Johnston, also declined to comment.
The speculation comes after IAG’s efforts to buy the Royal Automobile Club of Western Australia’s insurance business for $1.35bn were blocked by the Australian Competition and Consumer Commission, following IAG’s acquisition of RACQ’s insurance arm for $855m.
Suncorp is heavily weighted towards the Queensland market, and some say a deal could carry greater regulatory risk and political pressure from the Queensland state government should Tokio Marine acquire that business.
One analyst said both companies had a similar business mix, but IAG trades at a small premium to Suncorp with higher margins, owing to its motor club and reinsurance relationships.
Normally, Tokio Marine would target a specialty insurer focused on commercial lines, such as QBE, but it appears to be casting its net more broadly.
Japanese firms have been dissolving cross-shareholdings, creating a situation where they hold more capital to deploy outside Japan, and Tokio Marine has been vocal about looking at targets across Australia.
Japanese groups have previously bought Australian insurance businesses. Nippon Life owns the former MLC life insurance business and part of Resolution Life, while Dai-ichi bought Suncorp’s life insurance business for $725m in 2018.
For the six months to December, Suncorp reported a 76 per cent fall in net profit to $263m, on the back of higher natural hazard costs and lower investment returns. IAG, headed by Nick Hawkins, also reported a 35 per cent fall in half-year net profit on the previous corresponding period, to $505m.
